title: The Pacific Is Ground Zero for Deep-Sea Mining
gist: The Pacific has become the central testing ground for deep-sea mining (DSM) policy, with the US, China, and Japan racing to secure seabed mineral rights via bilateral deals while Pacific Island states split between courting investment and pursuing full moratoriums.

themes.theme: US policy reversal opens the field

insights.claim: Trump's April 2025 executive order directing acceleration of seabed mineral development marked a sharp reversal of prior US caution on deep-sea mining and has driven a wave of subsequent DSM activity across the Pacific.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A US policy shift on DSM removes a key regulatory brake and could accelerate commercial-scale seabed mining timelines, benefiting first-mover mining companies and their financiers.
insights.quote: accelerate the responsible development of seabed mineral resources
insights.locator: Background: From Nascent Industry to Headline News

insights.claim: The US is indicating willingness to pursue deep-sea mining in international waters by circumventing the International Seabed Authority (ISA), even though the US is not a UNCLOS signatory and has historically avoided moving beyond ISA rulings.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: If the US establishes a unilateral precedent for mining outside ISA jurisdiction, other countries and companies waiting on the sidelines could follow, effectively ending the multilateral moratorium-by-default that has held since exploration began.
insights.locator: The Road Ahead: U.S. Activity in International Waters

insights.claim: In 2025, The Metals Company (TMC), a Canadian firm, attempted to bypass the UN process entirely by applying for US-sponsored ocean mining permits in international waters, signaling that companies are willing to route around multilateral bodies when a permissive national regime is available.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Investors in DSM juniors should watch for regulatory arbitrage plays where companies seek permits from whichever government offers the fastest path, rather than waiting on ISA consensus.
insights.locator: Major Players in the Deep-Sea Mining Sector

themes.theme: Great power competition via seabed deals

insights.claim: Both the US and China signed separate deep-sea mining agreements with the Cook Islands within the same year, with the US offering a cooperative development framework and China a broader comprehensive strategic partnership, illustrating the two powers are competing head-to-head for the same small Pacific states.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Pacific microstates are becoming leverage points in US-China competition; expect more competing bilateral minerals/security packages offered to small island states with outsized EEZs.
insights.locator: Major Players in the Deep-Sea Mining Sector

insights.claim: Japan sent an exploration crew to Minamitori Island in January 2026 and, following PM Takaichi's March 2026 White House visit, announced expanded US-Japan cooperation on deep-sea critical minerals including rare earth muds around the island.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A US-Japan rare earth seabed alliance could create a non-China rare earth supply chain node worth tracking for critical minerals investors.
insights.locator: Major Players in the Deep-Sea Mining Sector

insights.claim: The US, Australia, and New Zealand would view with alarm any scenario where China's DSM projects come bundled with agreements granting Chinese vessels or companies greater access to Pacific maritime infrastructure, since that would accelerate the militarization/securitization of the region.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch Chinese DSM agreements for port-access or basing riders — a signal that minerals deals are being used as a wedge for broader strategic access.
insights.locator: The Road Ahead: Great Power Influence via DSM

insights.claim: American Ocean Minerals Corporation (AOMC), which recently merged with Odyssey Marine Exploration, holds investments in two of the three licensed exploration projects in the Cook Islands (Moana Minerals Ltd. and CIC Ltd.), positioning it as a leading challenger to The Metals Company's sector dominance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: AOMC's merger and dual Cook Islands stakes make it a name to track as a consolidator in an otherwise fragmented, pre-commercial DSM equity landscape.
insights.quote: celebrating a new golden age of American minerals
insights.locator: Major Players in the Deep-Sea Mining Sector

themes.theme: Pacific nations split on DSM policy

insights.claim: Naoero's (Nauru's) President David Adeang frames DSM opposition as the greater risk, arguing inaction on renewable-energy mineral supply is more dangerous than mining's environmental impact — an explicit pro-DSM framework used to justify small island state participation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Nauru's cost-benefit framing (climate mineral needs > seabed ecological risk) is a template other resource-poor small states could adopt to justify DSM licensing revenue.
insights.quote: the greatest risk we face is not the potential environmental impacts of mineral recovery but the risk of inaction
insights.locator: Background: From Nascent Industry to Headline News

insights.claim: New Caledonia has implemented one of the most restrictive anti-DSM policies in the Pacific: a 50-year ban on deep-sea mining across its entire maritime zone.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A 50-year ban effectively removes New Caledonia's large EEZ from the investable DSM universe for a generation.
insights.locator: Background: From Nascent Industry to Headline News

insights.claim: Australia, despite being a major land-based mining nation, has deliberately avoided taking a public stance on DSM — even omitting it from its Critical Minerals Strategy 2023-2030 — likely to avoid alienating any Pacific Islands Forum member while it pursues broader regional security agreements.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Australia's silence is itself a signal: expect Canberra to continue prioritizing regional security cohesion over taking sides on the DSM economic-vs-environment debate.
insights.locator: Background: From Nascent Industry to Headline News

insights.claim: The Cook Islands Seabed Minerals Authority is conducting broad impact assessments before deciding whether to grant extraction (not just exploration) licenses, despite already licensing three companies to explore its EEZ — making it the key bellwether case for whether frontier DSM moves from exploration to extraction.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The Cook Islands' extraction-license decision is a near-term catalyst investors in DSM licensees should watch closely, as it will set a template other Pacific states may follow.
insights.locator: The Road Ahead: How Forward-Leaning Pacific Countries Progress on DSM

insights.claim: The Pacific supplies up to 60 percent of the world's tuna, making the region's maritime resource base economically critical beyond minerals and raising the stakes of any DSM-related ecological damage to fisheries.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Any DSM-linked fisheries disruption carries outsized economic risk for Pacific economies dependent on tuna exports — a factor that could tip several island states toward moratorium positions.
insights.locator: Background: From Nascent Industry to Headline News

insights.claim: The DSM industry has not yet demonstrated that seabed mineral extraction is economically feasible at scale, even as a growing number of companies pursue exploration licenses — meaning current investment is speculative and pre-commercial.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Investors should treat DSM equities as exploration-stage/optionality plays, not production-ready assets, until commercial viability data emerges from ongoing testing.
insights.locator: Major Players in the Deep-Sea Mining Sector

insights.claim: Environmental risks from DSM include ocean noise pollution disrupting marine migration/reproduction, nutrient-poor waste plumes starving zooplankton and micronekton, and carbon release potentially weakening the ocean's temperature-moderating capacity — but the actual extent of these impacts remains scientifically unclear due to limited knowledge of deep-sea ecosystems.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Scientific uncertainty over environmental impact means regulatory outcomes remain highly unpredictable — a binary risk for DSM investors depending on how test results land.

insights.claim: Civil society groups including Greenpeace, Fa'asao Amerika Samoa, and the Conservation Council for Hawai'i are actively opposing DSM through petitions, conference interventions, and lawsuits against the US government, meaning Pacific governments must balance economic opportunity against social license risk.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Active litigation against the US government adds legal/regulatory risk to any US-territory DSM projects (American Samoa, CNMI) that investors should price in.

insights.claim: American Samoa, CNMI, and Guam all want at least a temporary ban on DSM in their own waters despite growing US federal government interest, creating tension between territorial governments and Washington.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US territorial resistance could slow federal DSM ambitions in the Pacific and create a template of leveraging bans for infrastructure concessions (ports, roads, health facilities) rather than mining revenue.
insights.locator: The Road Ahead: U.S. Pacific Territories Navigating DSM

insights.claim: Guam enacted a law allowing its port authority to deny port access to ships associated with seabed mining, an example of a territorial government asserting control over DSM-linked shipping despite lacking sovereign authority over mining policy itself.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Port-access restrictions are a concrete legal tool other Pacific jurisdictions could replicate to obstruct DSM logistics even without banning mining outright.
insights.locator: The Road Ahead: U.S. Pacific Territories Navigating DSM
